hints: Focus on the solvent for the sodium hydroxide, as aqueous and ethanolic conditions send halogenoalkanes down completely different pathways.
Remember that NaOH dissolved in ethanol acts as a base that removes H alongside the Cl, rather than as a nucleophile that replaces Cl.
Think about what happens when you remove HCl from a 3-carbon chain, and what functional group and name that unsaturated product will have.
walkthrough:
**Spot the Key Condition**

Great eye, the reagent is not just NaOH, it is NaOH dissolved in ethanol and heated under reflux. That little word ethanol changes everything.

Condition: $\text{NaOH in ethanol, heat}$

**Recall the Two Competing Pathways**

Halogenoalkanes have two classic reactions with hydroxide. Think of it simply as replace versus remove.

$$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Cl} + \text{OH}^- \text{(aqueous)} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH (substitution)}$$
$$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Cl} + \text{OH}^- \text{(ethanolic)} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CH=CH}_2 \text{ (elimination)}$$

**Apply to 1-Chloropropane**

Here we have ethanolic conditions, so hydroxide acts as a base. It pulls off a hydrogen from the adjacent carbon while chloride leaves, forming a C=C double bond.

$$\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Cl} + \text{NaOH (ethanol)} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{CH=CH}_2 + \text{NaCl} + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$

**Name the Type and Product**

Removing a small molecule like HCl to make an alkene is called elimination. The 3-carbon alkene is propene. That gives elimination plus propene.

options.A: Incorrect because it mixes the two pathways. Elimination does not make an alcohol, it makes an alkene by removing HCl. Propan-1-ol is the substitution product, not the elimination product.
options.B: Correct. Ethanolic NaOH causes dehydrohalogenation (elimination) of 1-chloropropane to form the alkene propene, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH=CH}_2$, plus NaCl and water.
options.C: Incorrect for these conditions, though it is a very tempting trap. Substitution to propan-1-ol happens with aqueous NaOH, where $\text{OH}^-$ acts as a nucleophile. With ethanolic NaOH, $\text{OH}^-$ acts as a base and elimination occurs instead.
options.D: Incorrect because the type and product do not match. Propene is correct for ethanolic conditions, but forming an alkene by loss of HCl is elimination, not substitution.
